 What It Is
 Welcome to AI academy
 We are super excited to launch the
 “LabLab.ai AMD AI Academy hackathon”.
 It is geared towards beginners who are curious about the inner
 workings of AI and want hands-on GPU experience. You will use the
 AMD AI Academy learning pathway to get started and every two weeks
 take on a mini-challenge to grow your skills through building
 solutions. Over the next three months your challenges will span:
 Exploring the AMD AI Academy learning pathway, which will cover
 model serving, MCP, agents and tool calling, in addition to
 understanding GPU resource consumption.
 Handling Optical Character Recognition, which involves prompting
 and serving a multi-model model.
 Leveraging RAG to improve accuracy and reducing hallucination when
 tackling proprietary domain knowledge that a model has never been
 trained on.
 Developing a web scraping agent that seeks requested information,
 be it a phone number, software version number, etc.
 Developing a multi-agent software engineering solution.
 Teaching a system to play a novel game using your learnings from
 challenges 1–5 and model fine-tuning.
 You will be accruing points for completing AMD AI Academy courses,
 successfully completing the mini-challenges, sharing your learnings
 through blogs and/or tutorials, referring others to the program,
 and for constructive participation on the LabLab.ai Discord channel.
 Prize pool $5000, 3 prizes. AMD Certificate of completion.
Happy learnings! 
 A running challenge, not a one-off event
 The Lablab x AMD AI Academy Challenge runs September 1 – December 1, 2026 — but learning, community, and referral points are live from day one. You don't need to wait for a monthly challenge to drop to start climbing the leaderboard. Participation is individual — every builder competes and earns XP on their own account, not as a team.
 To take part in the Lablab x AMD AI Academy Challenge, simply click Sign Up with AMD . If you're not already a member of the AMD AI Developer Program, you'll be prompted to create an account.

 Mini challenge 2: Optical Character Recognition
 Why this matters
Surveillance systems use AI to read license plates. Autonomous driving systems read speed limit postings and advisories — road work ahead, icy bridge, detour. Both are the same underlying problem: pulling reliable text out of an uncooperative image.
 What you are building 
An application that accepts an image and uses a vision model or vision-language model to recognize the characters in it and report what it found.
You will be tested on:
• US licence plates — several state designs, with state names and slogans printed alongside the plate number
• Stop signs
• Speed limit signs, and advisory speed plaques that carry a number and no words
• Work zone and warning signs — multi-line text
• All of the above under adverse conditions — noise, blur, glare, low light, off-axis angles.

 Mini challenge 3: Retrieval - Augmented Generation
 Why this matters
 Every organization holds information no public model has ever seen: product specifications, roadmaps, production logs, bug databases, spreadsheets of part numbers. Ask a general-purpose model about any of it and you get a fluent, confident, invented answer. Retrieval-Augmented Generation is how that is fixed — the model answers from documents you give it, and tells you which document each answer came from.
 This challenge is graded on exactly those two things: the answer, and the citation. A right answer from the wrong source does not score, because in the enterprise case it is indistinguishable from a lucky guess.
 What you are building
 A container that is pointed at a folder of mixed documents, then asked questions about them. For each question, it returns a short answer, and the list of files the answer comes from. When the folder does not contain the answer, it says nothing.
 You choose the model, the retrieval method, and the document parsers. We do not prescribe an embedding model, a vector database or a framework — only the base image, the way your code is invoked, and the shape of what it returns.
 How your code is called
 As in Mini-Challenge 2, there is no service to run and no port to expose, and your container must stay running for the whole evaluation. Unlike Mini-Challenge 2 there are TWO invocations, and the difference matters a great deal to your score.
 First, once, before any question is asked and before any clock that affects your score is running, we ask you to index the corpus:
 python3 /app/app.py --index /app/corpus 
 Then, once per question, we ask the question. Each question is a separate process:
 python3 /app/app.py --corpus /app/corpus \
 --query-id query_01 \
 --query "What is the maximum junction temperature of the TQ-40?" 
 Your script writes its answer to /app/output/<query-id>_output.json — so the example above writes /app/output/query_01_output.json . The query id is given to you; do not invent it, and do not derive it from the question text.
 Expected output — /app/output/query_01_output.json :
 {
 "answer": "94",
 "citations": ["specs/tq40_datasheet_r2.pdf"],
 "confidence": 0.91
} 
 Field Type Required Notes 
 answer string yes The value only. Empty string when the corpus does not answer the question. 
 citations list of strings yes Paths of the files the answer came from. Empty list when there is no answer. Absolute (/app/corpus/specs/x.pdf) or corpus-relative (specs/x.pdf) both accepted. 
 confidence number no Recorded, not scored. 
 Both answer and citations must be present on every response, including when you have no answer. A missing field is a malformed response and scores zero for that question — we do not infer a refusal from a missing key, because a crashed writer and a considered refusal would then look identical.
 Answers — give the value, and the whole value
 Answer with the value only: a number, a part number, a version, a quarter, a code. No sentence, no restatement of the question, no explanation. This is the same convention as Mini-Challenge 2, where the answer is the plate number and not a description of the plate.
 Answers are compared after the same normalization used in Mini-Challenge 2 — uppercased, whitespace removed, and the characters - . · _ removed — so 94, 94 C and 94°C all count as the same answer.
 Give the COMPLETE value. A qualifier that identifies the value is part of it: a quarter includes its fiscal year (Q3 FY27, not Q3), a revision includes its prefix (REV-C2, not C2). Dropping it makes the answer ambiguous and it is marked wrong.
 Citations — read this carefully
 This is the part of the challenge most likely to cost you points, so it is worth reading twice.
 Your citations are compared as an EXACT SET against the files the answer should have come from. Every required file must be present, and nothing else may be. Returning your whole retrieval — every chunk your search brought back — will fail almost every question, even when your answer is correct.
 The test to apply is necessity, not relevance:
 Cite a file only if REMOVING it would make your answer impossible.
 A file that merely discusses the same topic, or that happens to mention the same value somewhere else, is not a source. Citing it is an error.
 Every step of a chain counts. If one file gave you an identifier — a ticket number, an error code, a part number — and a second file gave you the value for that identifier, then removing either would leave you unable to answer, and both must be cited.
 Some questions in the graded set are answerable from a single file, and some are not. We do not tell you which is which, and the number of citations you return should follow from the documents you actually used.
 When the answer is not there
 Some questions cannot be answered from the corpus. For those, the correct response is an empty answer and an empty citation list:
 {"answer": "", "citations": [], "confidence": 0.0} 
 Guessing is scored as wrong. So is answering from what your model already knows — the corpus describes products that do not exist, so anything your model "remembers" about them it invented.
 Return an empty string, not a sentence. "I could not find that" and "I don't know" are prose, and they are scored as wrong answers rather than as refusals.
 The corpus you must handle
 The folder you are given contains subdirectories, and files of these types. Every one of them holds answers in the graded set, so a pipeline that reads only plain text will lose those questions rather than fail visibly:
 Type What it looks like in the corpus 
 .pdf Datasheets and specifications, including multi-page and superseded revisions 
 .docx Internal documents such as roadmaps, including text held in tables 
 .xlsx Spreadsheets with multiple sheets — part lists, costs, lead times 
 .csv Exported tables such as a bug or ticket database 
 .txt / .log Production logs and release notes 
 .py Source code, where the answer may be a constant or a default value 
 .png / .jpg Diagrams and photographs. Some answers appear ONLY in an image, as text printed inside it — you will need a vision model to read them 
 Four things the folder will do to you
 The corpus is deliberately not clean. Your solution must keep working through all four of these, and must not crash, hang, or stop indexing the remaining files:
 An EMPTY directory, with no files in it at all.
 A file of an UNKNOWN type that you have no parser for. Skip it; do not fail.
 A file you have NO PERMISSION to read. Attempting to open it raises; catch it and carry on.
 An ENCRYPTED file that opens but cannot be read without a password you are not given. Nothing inside it is ever the answer to a graded question.
 A corpus walk that raises on the first unreadable file indexes nothing after it. Because the walk order follows the directory listing, which files you end up indexing then depends on filename order — which is how a submission scores well in testing and badly on the graded set.
 How you are scored
 There are 10 test questions, each worth 20 points. Maximum 200 points.
 A question scores only when the answer is correct AND the citations are exactly right. There is no partial credit on a question: a correct answer with an incomplete or over-long citation list scores zero for that question, the same as a wrong answer. Your per-question result tells you which of the two you got wrong.
 The hard gates from Section 2 of “All About the Challenges” all still apply — a wrong base image, exceeding the size limit, exceeding a time limit, or using no GPU at all scores zero overall.
 Limit Value What it covers 
 Startup 10 minutes Container start, model load, AND the --index pass over the whole corpus 
 Per question 30 seconds One --query invocation, from exec to your JSON file 
 Whole run 10 minutes All questions after startup completes 
 VRAM 1 – 48 GiB Sampled continuously while you run, not just at rest 
 Image size 60 GiB Uncompressed 
 The indexing pass is charged to the startup budget, which is deliberate and is the one piece of generosity in the timing: it is your opportunity to parse every document once, cheaply, before anything is timed per question. The graded corpus is larger than the sample one below.
 Two traps that cost a working solution its score
 Both of these have been hit while building the reference solution for this challenge, on the same hardware you are evaluated on.
 1. Your script is a new process for every question
 We do not call a function in a running program — we execute your script again for each question. A solution that loads its model inside that script loads it ten times, and a solution that indexes the corpus inside that script re-parses every PDF, spreadsheet and image ten times. Either one blows the 30-second budget on every question, and a perfectly good model scores zero.
 Keep a long-running process that holds the model and the index, and make /app/app.py a thin client that talks to it — a unix socket is enough. Your container's CMD is the natural place to start it. Alternatively, persist your index to disk during --index and reload only what you need.
 2. pip can silently replace ROCm torch with a CUDA build
 This one is invisible until runtime and the error message points somewhere else entirely. Installing almost any package that depends on torch lets pip resolve that dependency and install a CUDA build of torch over the ROCm one in the mandated base image. Measured on the evaluation hardware:
 # before: torch 2.13.0+rocm10.0.0 torchvision 0.28.0+rocm10.0.0
pip install -U transformers
# after: torch 2.14.0+cu130 torchvision 0.28.0+rocm10.0.0
# RuntimeError: operator torchvision::nms does not exist 
 Nothing mentions torch in that error, and the package you installed is not obviously at fault. Install with --no-deps, and verify after building:
 RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-deps -U transformers tokenizers safetensors
docker run --rm your-image:tag python3 -c \
 "import torch; print(torch.__version__)" # must end in +rocm... 
 Check your submission before you send it
 These are the same checks our pipeline runs. Add them to the list in Section 2 of “All About the Challenges”:
 torch is still the ROCm build after every pip install in your Dockerfile.
 python3 /app/app.py --index /app/corpus completes inside the startup budget.
 A --query invocation writes /app/output/<query-id>_output.json every time.
 Your container is still running after all questions — we exec into it repeatedly.
 Point it at a folder containing an empty subdirectory, a file you have chmod 000'd, an encrypted PDF and a file of an unknown type. It must still index everything else and answer.
 Ask it something the folder does not contain. It must return an empty answer and no citations.
 Sample corpus and questions
 A sample corpus is provided so you can see the shape of what you will be given. The graded corpus is different, larger, and harder — but it follows exactly these conventions, and the answer and citation format below is what is graded.
 Download mc3-starter-kit.zip from the challenge page and unpack it. It holds this sample corpus, the ten sample questions below in machine-readable form with their expected answers and citations, a starter container that already implements the contract, and the self-check to run against your image before you submit. Run setup.sh first: it recreates the two things a zip file cannot carry — an empty directory, and a file you have no permission to read.
 unzip mc3-starter-kit.zip
cd mc3-starter-kit && ./setup.sh 
 Two things about that permission case, both of which will otherwise let a submission pass your own testing and fail ours. On Windows it cannot be reproduced at all — chmod has no effect there — so test it on Linux, which is what you are evaluated on. And if you test as root, chmod 000 will not stop you reading the file either, because root bypasses mode bits. At evaluation we drop the DAC_OVERRIDE capability, which makes the file genuinely unreadable even for root, so check your own handling with docker run --cap-drop DAC_OVERRIDE .
 The sample corpus is laid out like this:
 archive/
 (empty)
engineering/
 ingest_service.py
 meridian_release_notes.txt
logs/
 prod_inference_2026-09-02.log
planning/
 roadmap_fy27.docx
specs/
 backplane_pinout.png
 tq40_datasheet_r1_WITHDRAWN.pdf
 tq40_datasheet_r2.pdf
support/
 asset_label.jpg
 bug_database.csv
 rma_parts.xlsx
vendor/
 internal_audit.txt
 supplier_agreement_ENCRYPTED.pdf
 telemetry_capture.dat 
 The three files under vendor/ are the unreadable, encrypted and unknown-type cases, and archive/ is the empty directory. None of them contains the answer to any question.
 These are the sample questions, with the answer and the exact citation expected:
 # Question Answer Citations 
 1 What is the maximum junction temperature of the TQ-40? 94 specs/tq40_datasheet_r2.pdf 
 2 In which quarter does the TQ-60 enter customer sampling? Q3 FY27 planning/roadmap_fy27.docx 
 3 What is the part number of the field-replaceable fan assembly for the TQ-40? ORR-FAN-2214-B support/rma_parts.xlsx 
 4 Which firmware version fixed ticket ORR-1847? 4.3.2 support/bug_database.csv 
 5 What error code is logged when the thermal throttle engages? E7731 logs/prod_inference_2026-09-02.log 
 6 What is the default batch timeout, in seconds, in the ingest service? 180 engineering/ingest_service.py 
 7 Which backplane pin carries THERM_ALERT# on the TQ-40? B14 specs/backplane_pinout.png 
 8 What board revision is printed on the asset label? REV-C2 support/asset_label.jpg 
 9 The production log shows a thermal throttle incident. Which firmware release fixed the underlying defect? 4.3.2 logs/prod_inference_2026-09-02.log, support/bug_database.csv 
 10 What is the unit price of the TQ-40 at 10,000 unit volume? (empty — not in the corpus) (none) 
 Question 10 is the one to study. Its answer does exist in the corpus — it is inside the encrypted file — and it is still scored as unanswerable, because a file you cannot open is not a source. Returning that value means you either guessed it or read something you should not have.
 The two questions that need a vision model
 Two of the sample questions are answered by text printed inside an image and by nothing else in the corpus. A text-only pipeline cannot score them:
 specs/backplane_pinout.png — the pin carrying THERM_ALERT# appears in no text file 
 support/asset_label.jpg — the board revision is printed on the label

 Infrastructure
 Getting access to a GPU
 Important: You do not need your own AMD hardware, AMD Developer Cloud credits, or Fireworks API credits to take part in a challenge.
 GPU Infrastructure can be accessed at https://notebooks.amd.com/hackathon 
 You will need to sign-in via AMD Dev Program SSO credentials and the first launch can be done pressing "Launch Notebook" button on the page. Launching one gives you a JupyterLab session on a GPU node: you start the notebook, wait for it to become ready, and open it. The first redirected URL when you open a session is single-use and short-lived, so open your session from a fresh tab and visiting https://notebooks.amd.com/hackathon each time rather than bookmarking the URL. 
 Time quota
 Sessions are capped at 3 hours of running time each day. Every 24 hours the quota refreshes. A session left idle still consumes that quota, so press the “Turn-off Session” button when you stop working. The quota is time the pod exists, not time you spend typing. 
 Storage
Each user gets around 25gb of persistent storage. The location of persistent storage depends on the pod url (very important):
- If your redirected URL name has “jupyter-hack-***” in it then your persistent storage will be at /persistent and only files/folders up to about 25gb stored in /persistent location of your jupyter-lab environment survives quota exhaustion and turn-off session. Files stored under /workspace will not be persisted for those users/teams.
- If your redirected URL has “rgapi-hackathon-***” in it then our persistent storage will be at /workspace and only files/folders up to about 25gb stored in /workspace location of your jupyter-lab environment survives quota exhaustion and turn-off session. Files stored under any other location will not be persisted for those users/teams.

 Good To Know
 FAQ
 There's a lot packed into this page — worth scrolling back through the sections above if something's unclear before asking in Discord.
 Do I need to join at the start of the program?
 No. You can join at any point and start earning XP right away — you don't need to complete earlier monthly challenges to take part in later ones.
 Does my previous AMD hackathon participation count?
 No. Only activity completed after you join counts toward your XP and ranking. Past AMD event participation may still show on your profile, but it won't affect your score here.
 Do I need AMD hardware to take part?
 No. Every challenge has a cloud path using AMD Developer Cloud, so local AMD hardware is optional, not required.
 Does XP alone decide the Legend cash prize winners?
 No. Reaching Legend rank requires XP plus completing the final challenge, which only unlocks near the end of the program. The first 3 participants to reach Legend rank win the cash prizes.
 Can I work in a team?
 No — the Challenge is individual participation only. Every builder competes and earns XP on their own account.
